spec.cue: The view is grainy and wide, with ultraviolet flowers and flicker that the bee's eyes make visible.

cpd.note: honeybee workers resolve about 0.26 cycles per degree

fovea.note: no record gives a sharper middle for bees

fall.note: the app's guess for how sharpness falls with light; no record gives a curve for bees

uvBlue.note: the ultraviolet channel is shown in the blue channel, as the bee's colour mapping requires

glow.note: movement glows so that flicker is visible

rate.note: time runs slower to suggest a faster flicker rate

living.note: no extra weight for living movement

topoA.note: by analogy with the house cat

BEE.note: peaks near 340, 436 and 556 nm, from Apis mellifera records (Land 2012 gives 344, 436, 556; Kolyfetis 2025 gives about 340 nm)

field.name: squeeze
field.note: the wide field is squeezed toward the view's width

gaze.name: strip
gaze.note: the view scans in quick jumps

steady.name: lock
steady.note: the picture holds steady between jumps

saccade.note: quick head turns; 40 degrees and 4 frames are the app's choice

rows: A honeybee worker can resolve gratings of about 0.26 cycles per degree, roughly 1/230 of a person's detail.
Bees see close to 300 degrees around them, with the edges seen coarsely.
Bees have three kinds of colour receptor, peaking in the ultraviolet near 340 nm, in the blue near 436 nm and in the green near 556 nm.
Bumblebees turn their heads in quick jumps of 5 to 60 degrees, lasting 45 to 135 milliseconds, then hold gaze between turns.
The blur, the glow of movement, the brightness and the slowed time are the app's own choices, chosen to show how a bee's view differs. No record gives their values.

rows: A humpback whale resolves about 3.3 cycles per degree and a Bryde's whale about 4.8, both in water. The picture uses the humpback figure.
Dolphins see a panoramic field of 120 to 130 degrees, with their two eyes overlapping only a little. Their eyes sit to the side of the head.

Most whales have only rod cells in the dim light, so they see almost no colour. Where a green-sensitive pigment is recorded, a harbour porpoise or pilot whale reads about 520 nanometres, and the picture shows that green range.
Cetaceans have a reflective layer behind the retina. Seals have one too, and the picture lifts the shadows a little in the dark.
The gain, the fade of still things, the colour strength, the reflective sheen and the colour matrix are the app's own choices and have no record behind them.

claims.how: Set to 3.3 cycles per degree, the humpback value from the Lisney record, which lies between the two whale records.
Set to 125 degrees, the middle of the 120 to 130 degree dolphin range.

rows: Many monkeys and apes see three kinds of colour sensor; some New World species have only two, and owl monkeys see no colour at all.

A stumptail macaque with normal eyes resolves about 21 cycles per degree, close to a person's figure. A marmoset's fovea is estimated to resolve about 30. We blur the picture to about 21, the stumptail's figure.
Monkeys make small, quick eye movements even while they fix, averaging about half a degree. Microsaccades in rhesus monkeys average about 29 minutes of arc.
The sharp middle, the field width, the gain, the saturation, the frame rate and the picture's colour mapping are the app's choices, since no record gave them for these animals.

claims.how: The stumptail macaque's 1.4 arc minutes converts to 21.4 cycles per degree by 1 / (2 x 1.4/60), so the value is the record's converted figure.
